newsitem.title: GERMANY: Vargas Llosa urges sanctions on rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Vargas Llosa urges sanctions on rights abuses.

text.p: Peruvian novelist Mario Vargas Llosa urged the developed world to impose economic sanctions on countries which violate human rights, as he accepted Germany's top literary award during the Frankfurt Book Fair on Sunday.

The 60-year old Vargas Llosa, famed for his unsuccessful bid for his country's presidency six years ago, accused governments of turning a blind eye to human rights abuses in order to safeguard their investments in developing regions.
"This policy is immoral and also impractical," he said.

"The security of regimes which assassinate their dissidents, such as that of General Abacha of Nigeria, or a China which enslaves Tibet, or the tropical gulag of Cuba, is precarious and can collapse into anarchy and violence, as happened in the Soviet Union."
Vargas Llosa was speaking at a ceremony in Frankfurt's Paulskirche church at which he received the German Book Trade's Peace Prize for his lifelong efforts to promote a "culture of freedom."
In a congratulatory message, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl praised Vargas Llosa for his critiques and literary reflections on political developments.
"You have remained true to yourself throughout and preserved the freedom of your own judgement, irrespective of the Zeitgeist of the time," Kohl wrote.

A prolific essayist and author of 25 novels, Vargas Llosa is now estranged from his native Peru but remains a harsh critic of its authoritarian regime under President Alberto Fujimori, to whom he lost the 1990 elections.
The writer called on his peers to become more involved in the political arena and denounced the "increasing frivolity" which has debased literature into pure light entertainment.

The "paralysis" of the European Union over the recent crisis in Bosnia was dramatic proof of the dangers of complacency and demanded a vigorous initiative to arouse a sense of responsibility in people.

"Writers can contribute to this task, as they have in the past, when they still believed that literature was not just meant to entertain, but to arouse concern, to warn of danger and to inspire action for a good cause."
Vargas Llosa praised the award's "determination to view literary work as a responsibility which does not end on the artistic level."
Past winners of the German Peace Prize, worth 25,000 marks, include Czech Republic President Vaclav Havel.
Vargas Llosa, who now divides his time between London and Spain, says he has no more personal political ambitions.
At a news conference at the Frankfurt Book Fair on Saturday, he said: "I learned (from that) that I am an inept politician. I will stay doing what I do now, which is writing."
Vargas Llosa is one of the most widely-read Latin American writers.

Among his best known titles are: "The War of the End of the World," which describes a peasant revolt in 19th century Brazil and "Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter," a satire of Latin America's popular soap operas.
